notes: Ruling slot 18 = Revolutionary Command Council (Nimeiry). Coalition slot 19 = the pro-Nimeiry communist faction (Ahmed Suleiman, Mu'awiya Ibrahim) favouring merger into the regime; Mahjub's SCP stays in slot 4 as in MD. Nasserist Free Officers core in 7, Nile Valley unionists of the Tripoli Charter in 6, Ba'ath in 21 as in MD. Ansar of Imam al-Hadi in 9 (militant imamate, armed at Aba), Khatmiyya in 10 (accommodating establishment order), Umma Party in 14 and DUP in 1 as in MD. Southern actors: Anya-Nya 0 (Israeli/Western-backed), Southern Front 2, SANU 3. Native Administration as the monarchist slot.

0.name: Anya-Nya
0.text:
Anya-Nya is the guerrilla army of Southern Sudan, born in 1963 from veterans of the 1955 Torit mutiny and southern exiles, and named after a Madi word for snake venom. In early 1970 it is still divided among rival exile governments and local commanders, but Joseph Lagu, who controls the supply lines from Uganda and the arms delivered by Israel, is emerging as its dominant leader.

It fights for the self-determination of the three southern provinces against what it calls Arab domination and forced Islamization. Led by Christian, mission-educated men, it looks to Israel, Uganda, Ethiopia and Western churches for support and abhors the Soviet-armed regime in Khartoum. Its leverage lies in control of the bush and in southern grievances no Khartoum government has addressed.

1.name: al-Hizb al-Ittihadi al-Dimuqrati
1.text:
The Democratic Unionist Party was formed in December 1967 by the merger of Ismail al-Azhari's National Unionist Party and the People's Democratic Party of the Khatmiyya order. Banned with all parties after the May 1969 coup, it has lost its founder: Azhari, the father of independence, died in detention in August 1969, and Sharif Hussein al-Hindi has fled abroad to organize resistance.

It represents the urban middle classes, merchants and Khatmiyya followers of the north and east, and favours a parliamentary system, private enterprise and an Islamic constitution while rejecting communism. Its leverage lies in the Khartoum and Omdurman bourgeoisie, the trading towns along the Nile and its links to the conservative Arab monarchies.

2.name: Southern Front
2.text:
The Southern Front was founded in 1964 by southern intellectuals and civil servants in Khartoum, among them Clement Mboro, Hilary Paul Logali and Abel Alier, as the voice of the South inside the country. It represented the South at the 1965 Round Table Conference and won seats in parliament, and after the May coup some of its members, notably Abel Alier, accepted posts in the revolutionary government.

It seeks a negotiated peace, regional autonomy or federation for the South, equal citizenship, freedom of religion and of the press, and the rule of law rather than military rule from either side. Its base is the educated southern elite, the churches and the southern towns, and its leverage lies in being Khartoum's indispensable interlocutor for any settlement.

3.name: Sudan African National Union
3.text:
The Sudan African National Union was founded in exile in 1962 as the Sudan African Closed Districts National Union by Joseph Oduho, Father Saturnino Lohure and William Deng, and later split between an exile wing and Deng's internal party. Deng returned to contest the 1968 elections and was assassinated in May 1968; since the May 1969 coup the party is banned and its members are scattered between Khartoum, Kampala and the bush.

It stands for a federal Sudan in which the South governs itself, for parliamentary democracy, civil rights and the development of the neglected southern provinces, looking to the West and East Africa rather than to the Arab world. Its leverage lies among southern students, civil servants and Dinka communities.

4.name: al-Hizb al-Shuyu'i al-Sudani
4.text:
The Sudanese Communist Party, founded in 1946, is one of the strongest communist parties in the Arab world and Africa, rooted among railway workers, Gezira tenants, students and the professional elite. Under its secretary-general Abdel Khaliq Mahjub it backed the May 1969 coup and has sympathizers in the cabinet, including Joseph Garang, but Mahjub refuses to dissolve the party into the regime's planned single organization.

It calls for a national democratic revolution: land reform, nationalization of banks and foreign companies, autonomy for the South, workers' democracy and a firm alliance with the Soviet Union. Its leverage lies in the Sudan Workers' Trade Union Federation, the tenants' and student unions and its sympathizers among young officers.

5.name: al-Hizb al-Shuyu'i al-Sudani - al-Qiyada al-Thawriyya
5.text:
The Revolutionary Leadership is a pro-Chinese splinter that broke away from the Sudanese Communist Party in 1964, accusing Abdel Khaliq Mahjub of parliamentary illusions and of following Moscow's revisionism. Led by Yusuf Abdel Majid and a small group of former cadres, it survives as a clandestine sect outside the regime's alliance with the left.

It denounces the partnership with the May officers as a betrayal, insisting that only a people's war of workers and peasants can make a real revolution, and preaches the mobilization of the Gezira tenants and the rural poor. Its influence is confined to a few student groups, intellectuals and union militants, but it offers a radical home to those disillusioned with both the regime and the official communists.

6.name: Wahdat Wadi al-Nil
6.text:
Unity of the Nile Valley is the old dream of union between Sudan and Egypt, revived by the Tripoli Charter of 27 December 1969, which pledged Egypt, Libya and Sudan to work toward a federation. Its partisans range from pro-Cairo officers and veteran unionists of the Ashigga tradition to Nasserist intellectuals, and they find a sympathetic ear in Deputy Chairman Babiker Awadalla.

They want Sudan to merge its sovereignty into a revolutionary Arab federation under Nasser's leadership, with an Arab and Islamic identity, a single political organization and the closest military ties with Egypt and the Soviet Union. They distrust both the communists and the southern movements. Their leverage lies in Egyptian patronage and Nimeiry's own admiration for Nasser.

7.name: Harakat al-Dubbat al-Ahrar
7.text:
The Free Officers Movement is the clandestine network of nationalist officers that carried out the coup of 25 May 1969 and now forms the core of the Revolutionary Command Council. Within it, a Nasserist and anti-communist group around Khalid Hassan Abbas, Abul Gasim Mohamed Ibrahim, Mamoun Awad Abu Zeid and Zein al-Abdin Mohamed Ahmed Abdel Gadir controls the army, the police and the new security organs.

They believe in revolution from above: a strong state led by officers, Arab socialism on the Egyptian model, a single mass organization and Soviet arms, with no room for parties or an independent communist movement. Their leverage lies in command of the Khartoum garrison, the security apparatus and their direct line to Nasser.

8.name: al-Ikhwan al-Jumhuriyyun
8.text:
The Republican Brothers are the disciples of Mahmoud Mohamed Taha, an engineer and mystic who founded the Republican Party in 1945 and has since turned it into a religious reform movement. Condemned for apostasy by a sharia court in 1968, Taha welcomed the May coup as the end of the sectarian parties and the Islamic constitution campaign, and his followers preach openly in Omdurman and at the universities.

They teach the 'Second Message of Islam': the universal, egalitarian verses of Mecca should replace the legal rules of Medina, opening the way to full equality of women and non-Muslims, democratic socialism and peace. Small but disciplined, they attract educated men and women and offer a reformist alternative to both the Brotherhood and the sects.

9.name: al-Ansar
9.text:
The Ansar are the followers of the Mahdi, whose revolution overthrew Turco-Egyptian rule in 1885, and form the largest religious movement in northern Sudan. Their spiritual leader, Imam al-Hadi al-Mahdi, refuses to recognize the May regime and has withdrawn to the family stronghold of Aba Island on the White Nile, where thousands of armed followers are gathering around him.

They see the regime of officers and communists as godless and demand an Islamic constitution and a government guided by the Imam of the Ansar. Their strength lies in the masses of Kordofan, Darfur and the White Nile, in the Mahdi family's agricultural estates and in a tradition of jihad that makes them the regime's most dangerous enemy.

10.name: al-Tariqa al-Khatmiyya
10.text:
The Khatmiyya is the great Sufi order founded in the early nineteenth century by Muhammad Uthman al-Mirghani, whose descendants lead it as a hereditary religious aristocracy. Since the death of Sayyid Ali al-Mirghani in 1968, his son Muhammad Uthman al-Mirghani heads the order, which provided the religious backbone of the People's Democratic Party and now of the banned Democratic Unionist Party.

Historically pro-Egyptian and wary of Mahdist ambitions, the Khatmiyya prefers accommodation with whoever holds power and keeps its distance from Imam al-Hadi's defiance. It stands for orthodox piety, social conservatism and respect for religious notables. Its leverage lies in its followers in the north and east and among Khartoum's commercial class.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, has a small Sudanese following among students and teachers who encountered it in Jordan, Egypt and the Gulf. Its members meet in discreet study circles in Khartoum and Omdurman and circulate leaflets denouncing the May regime as a tool of atheist communism.

The party rejects nationalism, parliamentary politics and the Sufi sects alike and demands the restoration of a single caliphate ruling by sharia, to be achieved by winning over army officers. Tiny and secretive, it has none of the Brotherhood's mass base, but its uncompromising doctrine appeals to young men disillusioned by the failure of every Sudanese party.

12.name: Jabhat al-Mithaq al-Islami
12.text:
The Islamic Charter Front is the political arm of the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood, formed in 1964 after the October Revolution and led by Hassan al-Turabi, a London- and Sorbonne-trained dean of law. It won seats in the 1965 and 1968 elections and spearheaded the 1965 ban on the Communist Party and the campaign for an Islamic constitution; since the May coup it is banned and Turabi is in detention.

It seeks an Islamic state built on sharia, a modern Islamic economy and an educated vanguard leading society, rejecting both communism and the old sectarian leaderships. Its base is university students, young professionals and teachers, and its leverage lies in disciplined cells and its alliance with the Ansar against the regime.

13.name: al-Afandiyya
13.text:
Al-Afandiyya are the senior civil servants, judges, engineers and administrators trained at Gordon Memorial College and the University of Khartoum, who inherited the British administrative machine at independence. Every regime, from the parties to Abboud and now the May officers, has depended on them to run the ministries, the Gezira Scheme and the provinces, and the revolutionary cabinet itself is full of them.

They prize order, competence and continuity over ideology, distrust both sectarian patronage and communist mobilization, and prefer a neutral foreign policy that keeps aid flowing from East and West alike. Their leverage lies in their monopoly of administrative expertise, their hold on the public services and the fact that no government can rule Sudan without them.

14.name: Hizb al-Umma
14.text:
The Umma Party, founded in 1945 under the patronage of Sayyid Abd al-Rahman al-Mahdi, is the political vehicle of the Ansar and led Sudan's governments for much of the parliamentary era. Split since 1966 between the Oxford-educated modernizer Sadiq al-Mahdi and the traditionalist Imam al-Hadi, it was banned with all parties after the May coup, and Sadiq al-Mahdi is now under arrest.

It stands for Sudanese independence from Egypt, parliamentary rule, an Islamic constitution, private property and the great family estates, and a foreign policy tilted toward Britain and the conservative Arab states. Its base is the Ansar of the west and the White Nile, and its leverage lies in its electoral weight and the loyalty of the Mahdi family's followers.

15.name: Buyut al-Tijara
15.text:
The merchant houses are the great Sudanese business families, such as the Abu el-Ela and Osman Saleh houses, together with the Greek, Armenian and Syrian trading firms that dominate cotton export, import agencies and the first factories of Khartoum North. Their fortunes grew under the parliamentary governments and Abboud's regime, and they now watch with alarm as officers and communists talk of nationalizing banks and foreign trade.

They want private property protected, an open economy, credit and import licences, and a government that favours business over revolution, whether it looks to the West or to the Gulf. Their leverage lies in their control of trade and finance and in their ties to the unionist and Umma leaders.

16.name: al-Jallaba
16.text:
The Jallaba are the northern riverain traders who have spread across Kordofan, Darfur and the South, running shops, the gum arabic and cattle trade, lorries and money-lending in every market town. Independent, self-made and mobile, they form the commercial backbone of rural Sudan and resent controls imposed from Khartoum, from licences to fixed prices.

They want free markets, low taxes, open roads and an end to state monopolies, and they fear the regime's talk of cooperatives and state trading corporations. Politically they lean to the unionists, but their first loyalty is to trade. In the South and the west they are resented as agents of northern domination, yet their networks make them indispensable to the economy.

17.name: Hurras al-Dindir
17.text:
The Guardians of Dinder are the wildlife wardens, foresters and veterinary scientists who manage Dinder National Park near the Ethiopian border and the wildlife reserves of the South, together with the agronomists warning about the advance of the desert in Kordofan and Darfur. They form a small professional milieu within the forestry and wildlife services and the University of Khartoum.

They call for protecting wildlife from poaching and war, controlling overgrazing and charcoal cutting in the acacia belt, safeguarding the gum arabic forests and studying the vast schemes planned for the Nile and the Sudd before they are built. They have no mass base, but their warnings carry weight with donors and with a state that lives from agriculture.

18.name: Majlis Qiyadat al-Thawra
18.text:
The Revolutionary Command Council is the ruling body of the May Revolution, the coup of 25 May 1969 in which Gaafar Nimeiry and the Free Officers overthrew the parliamentary regime. Chaired by Nimeiry, who has also taken over as prime minister, it includes the civilian judge Babiker Awadalla and officers ranging from Nasserists to communist sympathizers such as Hashim al-Atta and Babikir al-Nur Osman.

It proclaims a Sudanese road to socialism: agrarian reform, nationalization of banks and foreign firms, an alliance of workers, peasants, intellectuals, soldiers and national capitalists, and regional autonomy for the South. Aligned with Nasser's Egypt and armed by the Soviet Union, it rests on the army, the left and popular enthusiasm for change.

19.name: Shuyu'iyyu Mayu
19.text:
The May Communists are the communist and fellow-travelling ministers and cadres who have thrown in their lot with Nimeiry, among them Ahmed Suleiman and Mu'awiya Ibrahim, against Abdel Khaliq Mahjub's insistence on an independent party. They argue that the May Revolution is a national democratic revolution in power and that communists should merge into the regime's planned single political organization, as Egyptian Marxists did in the Arab Socialist Union.

They favour rapid nationalizations, central planning, land reform and Soviet aid while accepting the officers' leadership and the regime's pan-Arab commitments. Their leverage lies in ministries, the press, the trade unions they have won over and Nimeiry's need for a loyal left.

20.name: Mu'tamar al-Beja
20.text:
The Beja Congress was founded in 1958 by educated Beja of the Red Sea Hills and Kassala to defend the most neglected people of eastern Sudan, and in 1965 it sent its own deputies to parliament. Banned since the May coup, it relies on Beja tribal leaders, students and the dock workers of Port Sudan.

It rails against the riverain elite of Khartoum that monopolizes power and wealth, and demands schools, water, health care and jobs for the east, a fair share of the port's revenue and a federal system for the regions. Its rhetoric is populist and fiercely local, suspicious of Arab nationalist ideology, and its leverage lies in uniting the Beja clans along the Red Sea route on which Sudan's trade depends.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki - Qutr al-Sudan
21.english: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Region of Sudan
21.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki - Qutr al-Sudan
21.text:
The Sudanese branch of the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party took shape in the 1960s among students returning from Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo and among teachers in Khartoum and the northern towns. Small, clandestine and divided by the 1966 schism between the Syrian and Iraqi wings, it rejects the May regime's Nasserist leanings and its alliance with the communists.

It preaches the unity of the Arab nation, a revolutionary vanguard party, Arab socialism and the Arabization of Sudanese identity, including the South. Its cult of party and nation, its militarism and its contempt for pluralism make it the hardest current of Arab nationalism. Its leverage lies in student unions, schools and contacts inside the officer corps.

22.name: al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Sudaniyya
22.text:
The Sudanese Armed Forces grew out of the British-officered Sudan Defence Force and have seized power twice, under General Ibrahim Abboud in 1958 and with the May coup of 1969. Since then the new rulers have retired many senior officers, and the army fights Anya-Nya in the South with fresh Soviet weapons while its officer corps is divided between Nasserists, communists and quietly conservative professionals.

As an institution it values unity, discipline and national integrity above ideology and sees itself as the ultimate guardian of the state against sectarian parties, southern separatism and chaos. Its leverage is decisive: no government in Khartoum survives without the loyalty of the garrisons, the armoured corps and the paratroopers.

23.name: al-Idara al-Ahliyya
23.text:
The Native Administration is the system of hereditary sultans, nazirs, meks and omdas through which the British ruled rural Sudan and which independent Sudan has preserved. The Sultan of Dar Masalit, the meks of the Nuba Mountains, the Baggara and Kababish nazirs and the Beja chiefs still collect taxes, judge disputes and deliver their people's votes, while the regime's left denounces them as feudal relics.

They stand for royal and tribal authority, customary law, the old hierarchies of lineage and land, and a Sudan governed through its traditional rulers rather than parties or commissars. Their leverage lies in the countryside, where most Sudanese still look first to their sultan or nazir, and in their alliances with the Umma Party and the Ansar.
